title: Students’ Perceptions to a Large Language Model’s Generated Feedback and Scores of Argumentation Essays
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model (LLM)-generated feedback on students’ written scientific argumentation in physics is perceived as useful and accurate, and whether LLM-assigned essay scores align with students’ performance on related physics multiple-choice questions. The motivating problem is that in large-enrollment introductory STEM courses, giving timely, individualized feedback on open-ended student reasoning is difficult, even though such feedback is important for developing problem-solving and metacognitive skills.

The study used OpenAI’s GPT-4o to generate delayed feedback and rubric-based scores for students’ written scientific arguments on two online quiz questions in an introductory calculus-based physics course. Students had been trained across the semester in claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) scientific argumentation through progressively reduced scaffolding in recitation. After students completed quiz bonus questions requiring a 50-word written scientific argument about their solution process, their responses were processed through the GPT-4o API with a prompt directing the model to give concise physics-focused feedback and a score out of 5 based on a rubric. Students later viewed the feedback and completed a post-survey rating its usefulness and accuracy, with additional open-ended comments collected for future analysis.

The population consisted of undergraduate students, primarily future engineers, enrolled at a large Midwestern U.S. land-grant university. The intervention occurred in the context of a first-semester calculus-based physics course, with argumentation tasks embedded in online quizzes during the last five weeks of the semester. Reported quantitative data included 730 students for Quiz 08 and 565 students for Quiz 09. The study was conducted at a single institution in the United States.

The authors conclude that LLM-generated feedback appears viable for supporting written scientific argumentation in large-enrollment physics courses. Students generally rated the feedback as mostly useful and mostly accurate, regardless of whether they answered the associated multiple-choice item correctly. LLM-assigned essay scores also differed in expected ways between students who answered harder or easier quiz items correctly versus incorrectly, suggesting the scoring was sensible. However, the study is exploratory and limited by delayed feedback delivery, lack of comparison to human feedback in the current analysis, and absence of evidence about actual learning gains from the feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model used here to generate scores and written feedback on student essays.
identified_tools.use_case: ChatGPT (via GPT-4o API) was prompted with the physics problem, an ideal answer, and a rubric to score students' written scientific argumentation essays out of 5 and provide up to 100 words of delayed feedback focused on physics concepts in an introductory physics course.

findings.finding_summary: For Quiz 08, ChatGPT-generated argumentation scores were higher for students who answered the related multiple-choice physics question correctly than incorrectly: correct M=2.14 (SD=1.24) vs incorrect M=1.12 (SD=1.11), with p<<0.001 and Cohen's d=0.87. The full quiz sample was N=730, and the overall ChatGPT score average was 1.69/5 (SD=1.29).
findings.measure: LLM-generated rubric scores on written scientific arguments, compared by correctness on related multiple-choice physics item (Quiz 08)

findings.finding_summary: For Quiz 09, ChatGPT-generated argumentation scores were also higher for students who answered the related multiple-choice item correctly: correct M=2.77 (SD=1.08) vs incorrect M=2.53 (SD=1.04), with p=0.015 and Cohen's d=0.22. The full quiz sample was N=565, and the overall ChatGPT score average was 2.72/5 (SD=1.08).
findings.measure: LLM-generated rubric scores on written scientific arguments, compared by correctness on related multiple-choice physics item (Quiz 09)

findings.finding_summary: Across both quizzes, the majority of students rated ChatGPT feedback as 'mostly useful' and 'mostly accurate' on post-survey Likert scales. The paper reports no significant difference in perceived usefulness or accuracy between students who got the multiple-choice question correct versus incorrect, but does not report exact counts, test statistics, or survey sample size.
findings.measure: Student perceptions of usefulness and accuracy of LLM-generated feedback via Likert-scale post-survey

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory primary study using descriptive statistics, group comparisons, and student perception surveys rather than a randomized or strong quasi-experimental design. It provides empirical evidence, but outcomes are largely perceptual and correlational.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports one large observed difference in AI-generated scores between correct and incorrect students on Quiz 08 (Cohen's d=0.87) and a small positive difference on Quiz 09 (d=0.22). Because at least one reported effect is medium-to-large, the impact tier is blue.
